newsitem.title: USA: Dow slumps as stocks stagger at end of record week.
newsitem.headline: Dow slumps as stocks stagger at end of record week.

text.p: Wall Street stocks staggered lower on Friday, retreating from their dizzying heights at the end of a record-shattering week.
The Dow slid 130 points to close unofficially at 7890. The decline pulled the blue-chip average to a slight loss for the week, despite its historic run on Wednesday past the 8000 milestone.
Tech stocks, which had paced the market's recent rally, were the leaders on the way down, taking their cue from Microsoft Corp, which fell nine points to 140-1/2.

Microsoft late Thursday reported fourth-quarter earnings that barely beat Wall Street estimates. Expectations had been running extremely high, propelling shares in the software company up 20 points in the week ahead of the report.
With Microsoft having merely a very good quarter -- instead of a great one -- investors opted to cash in some gains rather than attempt to continue bidding the market higher.
"Without a doubt, it's profit-taking," said Frank Calta, managing director of institutional trading at Dain Bosworth. "People used Microsoft as an excuse to sell."

Stocks were also hurt by a weak tone in the bond market, where attention turned to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semiannual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to Congress, scheduled for next Tuesday.
Analysts, who pore over the Fed chairman's every utterance, will watch for echoes of earlier ruminations on market bubbles and "irrational exuberance."

"This market is nervous right now," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "If Greenspan was concerned about a bubble with the Dow at 6200, what's he going to think at 8000?"
Amid the broad decline, investors could draw some encouragement from the recent surge of market activity, even through the traditionally slow summer season.

New York Stock Exchange volume nearly reached 600 million shares Friday, pushing weekly volume past 2.9 billion shares and smashing the previous record of 2.82 billion shares for the week ended January 24, 1997.
"Given where we are in the summer, I thought that was particularly impressive," said Peter Green, vice president of technical research at Gruntal & Co.
"Markets tend to get in trouble during periods of light selling and no buying, and this showed buyers were still active," he said.
Among individual issues, Motorola Inc fell seven points to 82, a day after its annual analysts' meeting.

During the meeting, Motorola executives said margins on the company's paging business were likely to shrink. On Friday, investment firm Robertson Stephens downgraded the shares, based in part on the meeting's cautious tone.
Stanley Works fell 2-1/16 to 44-7/16 after the company announced a steep second-quarter loss.
The loss included several charges related to a restructuring unveiled Friday. Stanley Works said it planned to cut 4,500 jobs and close nearly half its facilities.
America Online Inc fell 3-3/4 to 64 after Goldman Sachs removed the online service provider from the firm's Priority List of investments.
The S&P 500 fell 16.31 points to 915.30.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 20.86 points to 1547.99.
((-- Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730))
